passage:
"Mumma, sit. SIT. I'll make your tea." Nandini put her hands on her hips.
"Nandini, you can't use the stove."
"Then I'll get the biscuits. You lie down. Don't cry today, okay?"
Shalini swallowed. "Beta, you don't have to look after me."
"Yes I do. Yesterday you cried and slept all day."
Nani came in from the balcony. "Nandini, come. Biscuits are my job. Your job is to play."
"But who will watch Mumma?"
"I will. I'm staying all this week, every day. And Mumma is seeing her doctor on Friday."
Nandini hesitated. "Every day?"
"Every day. You can check each morning."
Nandini climbed into Nani's lap.

qa.q: Who says she will be there every day this week?
qa.a: Nani says she is staying all week, every day.

qa.q: What might Nandini be worried about when she tells Mumma, "Don't cry today"?
qa.a: She may be worried that her mother will cry and sleep all day again, so she tries to take charge.

qa.q: What choice did Nani make, and why does it help Nandini?
qa.a: Nani took over the grown-up jobs and promised to be there every day, giving Nandini a steady adult so she can be a child again.

qa.q: How might Shalini feel when her five-year-old tries to look after her?
qa.a: She may feel touched but also sad and worried, since she doesn't want her daughter carrying her.

grounding: A five-year-old bossily takes care of her struggling mother, and her grandmother steps in as a steady, consistent adult.

passage:
Class note, UKG-B, by Sharmila.
Payal, five, spent the morning managing everyone. "Ma'am, sit here. No, not there. Give me the chalk." At story time she clung to my sari, then hit my arm and ran to the corner. Ten minutes later she was back, stroking my hand. Her mother told me things at home have been very up and down lately.
What I did: kept my voice the same each time, kept the routine exactly as the chart shows, and said "I'm still here" after the hitting.
This afternoon I spoke to our school counsellor; we meet Payal's mother on Monday.

qa.q: What did Payal ask for at the start of the morning?
qa.a: She asked for the chalk.

qa.q: What might Payal be feeling when she clings, then hits, then strokes Sharmila's hand?
qa.a: She seems to need Sharmila badly but also feel unsafe about it, so she swings between holding on and pushing away.

qa.q: Which of Sharmila's choices helps Payal most, and why?
qa.a: Keeping the same calm voice and routine, and saying "I'm still here" after the hitting, shows Payal an adult who stays predictable.

qa.q: How might Payal's mother feel at Monday's meeting?
qa.a: She may feel anxious, but also supported, since the school is working with her rather than blaming Payal.

grounding: A teacher notes a child who bosses adults and swings between clinging and hitting, and responds with calm consistency and help from the counsellor.

passage: In the Byculla flat, Rafiq stood over his mother with a plate of bread. "Mama, eat now. Then lie down. No crying." Elizabeth had stayed in bed since morning again. He pulled the curtain shut, bossy as a nurse, then suddenly hit her arm and clung to it. At the door, the neighbour, Mrs D'Souza, who had brought dal, saw it all. She sat with Rafiq on the step, told him he had done a big job and didn't have to do it alone, and that evening phoned his aunt to come and stay, and called the child helpline for advice.

qa.q: What did Rafiq bring his mother?
qa.a: A plate of bread.

qa.q: What might Rafiq be feeling as he bosses his mother and then clings to her arm?
qa.a: He seems worried and scared, trying to take control because home feels unpredictable, while still needing comfort.

qa.q: What did Mrs D'Souza do that helped?
qa.a: She told Rafiq he didn't have to do it alone and, that evening, called his aunt and the child helpline.

qa.q: How might Elizabeth feel being told to eat by her small son?
qa.a: Elizabeth may feel ashamed or overwhelmed, aware that Rafiq is caring for her.

grounding: Shows a young child who bossily manages and cares for a parent, swings between hitting and clinging, and needs safe adults.

passage:
"Irawati-ma'am, you sit HERE. I'm giving the crayons."
"I can see you want to be in charge, Dhruv. Today the helper is Mitali."
"No! I do it. At home I make Papa's tea and tell Mummy when to stop crying."
Irawati knelt. "That's a lot of jobs."
Dhruv smacked her hand, then gripped it tight. "Don't go to the staff room."
"I'm not going. I'm here till the bell, same as every day. You're helper on Thursday; it's on the chart."
He let go slowly and sat. After school, Irawati wrote down his words and took them to the school counsellor.

qa.q: When will Dhruv be the helper?
qa.a: On Thursday; it's on the chart.

qa.q: What might Dhruv be feeling when he smacks and then grips Irawati's hand?
qa.a: He seems anxious and afraid she will leave, swinging between anger and clinging.

qa.q: What did Irawati do that a steady adult should do?
qa.a: She stayed calm, kept the same routine and promise, and took his words to the school counsellor that day.

qa.q: How might Mitali see Dhruv's demand to give out the crayons?
qa.a: Mitali might feel pushed aside or confused, not knowing why Dhruv needs to be in charge.

grounding: Illustrates a child who bosses a teacher and cares for parents at home, swings between hitting and clinging, and meets a steady adult.

passage: Home-visit note, week three. Hemant met me at the door and announced, "I'll make the tea for Binita-aunty. She gets tired." He fetched her slippers, told her when to sit, then scolded her for putting the sugar in first. When she laughed and hugged him, he hit her shoulder, then clung to her dupatta and wouldn't let go. Binita stayed calm, kept the same bedtime story and the same breakfast, and gently took back the kitchen jobs: "Grown-ups make tea here." Next step: I have booked play sessions with the child counsellor, and I will visit again on Friday.

qa.q: What did Hemant offer to make?
qa.a: The tea for Binita-aunty.

qa.q: What might Hemant be feeling when he hits Binita and then clings?
qa.a: He seems unsure and scared of closeness, wanting comfort but not trusting it yet.

qa.q: Which of Binita's choices will help Hemant most, and why?
qa.a: Keeping the same routines and calmly taking back adult jobs, because it shows him a grown-up can be steady and in charge.

qa.q: How might Binita feel when Hemant scolds her about the sugar?
qa.a: She seems amused and patient, but may also feel sad that he feels he must manage adults.

grounding: Shows a child who acts as caregiver and swings between hitting and clinging, with a calm, consistent adult and professional support.

passage:
At the village anganwadi, Sudha ordered the other children about: "Sit! Eat!" Some days her mother, Pooja, stayed in bed, and Sudha brought her water and told her to eat.
That morning Sudha clung to Jyoti Didi's sari, then suddenly slapped her hand and ran off.
Jyoti Didi didn't shout. She kept the day the same: songs, roti, drawing. "I'm here after drawing too."
That afternoon she walked Sudha home, sat with Pooja on the step and gently asked how she was managing. Then she called the ASHA worker, who agreed to visit next morning.

qa.q: What did Sudha bring her mother on bad days?
qa.a: She brought her water and told her to eat.

qa.q: What might Sudha have been feeling when she clung and then slapped?
qa.a: She seemed torn between needing Jyoti Didi and being afraid to rely on anyone, so she clung, then pushed away.

qa.q: What did Jyoti Didi do that gives Sudha a safe, steady adult?
qa.a: She stayed calm, kept the day's routine the same, told Sudha she would still be there, and that same afternoon checked on Pooja and called the ASHA worker.

qa.q: What might home be like for Pooja on days she stays in bed?
qa.a: Pooja may feel low and unable to cope, and may be relieved when someone asks gently how she is managing.

grounding: Shows a young child who bosses and cares for her mother and swings between clinging and hitting, and a steady adult who brings in help.
